name: Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System

clinicalPearls: Brain tumors of any histology tend to present with a mixture of generalized features (headache, nausea/vomiting, cognitive decline, personality change, gait disturbance from raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus) and focal features (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field defect) (Harrison 22e p.716).

The classic morning-predominant brain tumor headache that eases through the day is actually seen in only a minority of patients; tumor headaches may be holocephalic, ipsilateral to the lesion, or even migraine-like with throbbing pain and scotoma (Harrison 22e p.716).

Seizures occur in roughly 25% of patients with brain metastases or malignant gliomas but are the presenting symptom in up to 90% of low-grade gliomas; all tumor-related seizures have a focal onset whether or not that is clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.716).

Contrast (gadolinium) MRI is the preferred diagnostic study; CT is reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI. Neuroimaging is generally the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumor, and laboratory tests are rarely useful (Harrison 22e p.716).

Malignant tumors (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, show central necrosis, and are ringed by white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen on FLAIR sequences (Harrison 22e p.716).

Meningiomas are dural-based enhancing extra-axial masses with a characteristic dural tail that compress but do not invade brain; their principal differential is a dural metastasis or dural lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.716, p.722).

Adult diffuse gliomas are now classified molecularly: IDH-mutant astrocytoma (1p/19q intact), IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma (1p/19q co-deleted), and IDH wild-type glioblastoma; these molecular markers carry major prognostic weight (Harrison 22e p.718-719).

An unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts relative temozolomide resistance and a worse glioblastoma prognosis; MGMT promoter hypermethylation (gene silencing) predicts better response (Harrison 22e p.720).

Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumor (~35%), are more common in women and with prior cranial irradiation and NF2, and many are found incidentally; small asymptomatic ones can simply be monitored with serial MRI (Harrison 22e p.721-722).

Most brain metastases lodge at the gray-white junction in watershed territories; ~85% are supratentorial and ~15% in the posterior fossa, and distribution roughly mirrors regional blood flow (Harrison 22e p.723).

Melanoma has the greatest propensity to seed the brain (found in ~80% at autopsy), but lung and breast carcinomas are the most common sources overall; prostate and breast cancers also favor dural metastases that can mimic meningioma (Harrison 22e p.723).

In epidural spinal metastasis, back pain is the presenting symptom in virtually all patients and may precede neurologic signs by weeks to months; the pain characteristically worsens on lying down, in contrast to arthritic pain which eases with recumbency (Harrison 22e p.725).
Any cancer patient with severe back pain should undergo whole-spine MRI; plain films, bone scan, or CT may show bony disease but only MRI reliably delineates epidural tumor (Harrison 22e p.725).
harrison.pathophysiology: Most primary brain tumors have no identified cause; established risk factors are limited to ionizing radiation exposure (meningiomas, gliomas, schwannomas) and immunosuppression (primary CNS lymphoma), while electromagnetic field/cell-phone exposure, head injury, dietary N-nitroso compounds, and occupational factors are not proven. Tumors arise through a multistep accumulation of genetic alterations: loss of tumor-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of proto-oncogenes (EGFR, PDGFR), producing uncontrolled growth; many gliomas show marked molecular heterogeneity. The 2016 and 2021 WHO classifications integrate molecular parameters (e.g., IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, H3 K27/G34 alterations) with histology. Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the gray-white junction; leptomeningeal disease reaches the subarachnoid space via arterial circulation or retrograde venous flow and may also follow resection of a cerebellar metastasis. Epidural cord compression generally results from metastases to the axial skeleton (typically breast and prostate), though lymphoma can invade through an intervertebral foramen without bone destruction (Harrison 22e p.717, p.719, p.723, p.724-725).

additionalInvestigations: Gadolinium-enhanced cranial MRI (preferred for all suspected brain tumors); CT only if MRI not possible
FLAIR sequences to detect non-enhancing low-grade glioma and infiltrative disease

Whole-spine MRI (or CT myelography if MRI impossible) for suspected epidural cord compression
redFlags: New focal neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field loss) that is subacute and progressive
New-onset focal seizures, especially in an adult without prior epilepsy
Severe back pain in a cancer patient (suggests epidural metastasis) — warrants urgent whole-spine MRI
Leg weakness, sensory level, or sphincter dysfunction suggesting evolving spinal cord compression (a neuro-oncologic emergency)
New limb pain in a patient with breast, lung cancer, or melanoma (consider leptomeningeal spread)
Signs of raised intracranial pressure / hydrocephalus (worsening headache, vomiting, declining consciousness)
Multilevel neuraxis signs (combined cranial neuropathies plus radiculopathies) suggesting leptomeningeal carcinomatosis
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is highly histology- and molecular-subtype-dependent. Low-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas have median survival around 10 years (most eventually transform to higher grade); oligodendrogliomas (1p/19q co-deleted) generally exceed 10 years. Glioblastoma carries a poor prognosis with median survival in the 15-18 month range with combined therapy and ~10% 5-year survival; adverse factors are older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor Karnofsky status, and unresectable tumor. H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma has a median survival of roughly 1 year regardless of grade; H3 G34-mutant hemispheric glioma about 18-22 months. Medulloblastoma achieves long-term survival in ~70% but often with neurocognitive cost, varying by molecular subgroup (WNT best; group 3 worst). Completely resected meningiomas and schwannomas can be cured. Brain metastases treated with whole-brain radiotherapy alone yield median survival of only ~4-6 months, though stereotactic radiosurgery achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure. Leptomeningeal metastasis is treated palliatively with no curative therapy. In epidural metastasis, patients fare well if treated before a severe deficit develops, but overall survival is often short owing to widespread systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.718-725).
pitfalls: Assuming a tumor headache must be morning-predominant — most are not, and tumor headaches can mimic migraine.
Misattributing frontal-lobe apathy and withdrawal to primary depression rather than tumor.
Giving glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL — their cytolytic effect on lymphoma cells can yield non-diagnostic tissue.

Relying on a single CSF cytology in suspected leptomeningeal disease — it is positive in only ~50% on first lumbar puncture and still misses ~10% after three samples; imaging is diagnostic in only ~75%.
Forgetting that the smallest brain metastases can produce extensive edema while large ones cause little, and that imaging appearance is nonspecific.
Overlooking that ~10% of systemic cancers can first present with a brain metastasis, sometimes requiring biopsy of the brain lesion when no accessible systemic site exists.
Treating low-grade glioma as benign — most ultimately transform to higher grade.
Delaying spine imaging in a cancer patient with back pain until neurologic deficits appear.
harrison.severityClassification: Gliomas are graded by the WHO into grades 2-4 (low- vs high-grade) integrating histology with molecular markers (IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion; CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion upgrades an IDH-mutant astrocytoma to grade 4). Meningiomas are WHO grade I (benign), II (atypical), or III (malignant). Brain tumor symptoms are categorized as generalized (raised-ICP related) versus focal/lateralizing. Nervous-system metastatic disease is grouped clinically into intraparenchymal brain metastases, leptomeningeal (carcinomatous meningitis) metastases, and epidural spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.716, p.719, p.722).
management: Pursue maximal safe surgical resection or debulking, or stereotactic biopsy, to obtain integrated histological and molecular diagnosis
Deliver radiotherapy, using fractionated external-beam treatment for gliomas and stereotactic radiosurgery or whole-brain radiotherapy for metastases
Give chemotherapy tailored to molecular subtype, such as temozolomide for glioblastoma guided by IDH and MGMT status
Use corticosteroids such as dexamethasone to reduce peritumoural oedema and raised intracranial pressure, withholding them before biopsy when CNS lymphoma is suspected
Control tumour-related seizures with antiepileptic drugs
Treat brain metastases with local therapy while controlling the systemic primary tumour
Coordinate a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team with integrated molecular pathology to guide treatment and prognosis
Provide rehabilitation, supportive care, and timely palliative care
